before: OEDIPUS. Stern-faced queens — since coming to this land I have bent my knee first at your sanctuary. Do not frown on me, or on Phoebus. When he long ago told me all the miseries still to come, he also spoke of this respite, after many years: a refuge in a far-off land, a rest granted at last by dread divinities. "There," he said, "you shall round off your weary life — a blessing to the land you settle in, and a curse to the land that cast you out." He promised signs would come to mark my fate: earthquake, or thunderclap, or flash of lightning. And now I recognize the sign as yours — the sign that guided my wanderings into this grove of yours. Otherwise I would never have come upon you first, a man without wine for an offering, resting on your native rock. Goddesses, fulfill Apollo's word. Grant me some final resolution of my life, if I do not seem altogether vile, a slave to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear me, gentle daughters of primeval Night. Hear, city that bears the name of great Pallas — Athens, first of cities, pity this dishonored shade, the ghost of the man who once was Oedipus.

before: ANTIGONE. Sirs! You would not have turned away my blind father if, though gracious and inclined to pity, you knew the deeds he committed — not innocent, but done with no evil intent. Still, listen to a girl's plea for him, a girl who pleads for him alone. My eyes are not robbed of sight. They plead with you as a daughter's eyes can. You are our only hope — do not drive us from here! With one gracious nod, grant us this mercy we had almost given up on. Hear us, hear us — by all that you hold dear: wife, children, home, hearth, and God! Search as hard as you like — where will you find a single man who escapes destruction if a god drives him on?

before: CHORUS. Look! Where is he? Look around! Search every corner, every nook! That all-presuming man — where has he gone? Search the ground! A traveler, I'd say, a traveler and no native of ours — that old man must have been. Never would one of our people dare to provoke the Powers, or set foot in their sanctuary — the Maidens before whom every mortal trembles, whose name no voice utters, no cry names. before: OEDIPUS. Then may the gods never quench their deadly feud, and may it be my judgment that decides the fight they are now arming for, spear against spear — so that neither the one who now holds the scepter may keep the throne, nor the one who fled may return. They never raised a hand when I, their father, was thrust from hearth and home. When I was outlawed and banished, what did they care? Will you say it was done at my own request, a favor the state granted because I wished it? Not so. Mark this: on the very day when in the storm of my soul I craved death — even death by stoning — no one stepped forward to carry out that wild longing. But later, when time had dulled my anguish, and I felt that my rage had overrun those old mistakes — that was when the city set itself to drive me out by force, after sparing me for years. And my sons, who as sons should have helped, did nothing. One little word from them was all I needed, and they did not speak a word. They let me wander on forever, a banished man, a beggar. These two girls, their sisters, gave everything their sex could give — food, safe shelter, a daughter's care — while their two brothers sacrificed their father for the lust of power and the scepter of kingship. No — they shall never have me for an ally, and this Theban kingship will bring them no gain. I know this from this girl's oracles, and from those old prophecies about me that Phoebus has now at last brought to pass. Let Creon come, then. Let all the mightiest in Thebes come seeking me. For if you, my friends, championed by those dread local Powers, take up my cause, then you gain for the State a great deliverer, and for my enemies a curse.

before: THESEUS. I had often heard of you in the past — the bloody mutilation of your eyes — and so I recognize you, son of Laius. Everything I gathered on the way here made my guess doubly certain. And now your clothes and that ruined face prove it: you are the man. So, pitying your condition, most ill-starred Oedipus, I want to know what you are asking of me and of Athens — you, and the helpless girl at your side. Speak. The tale would have to be grim indeed for me to recoil from it. I too was raised in exile, like you, and wrestled in foreign lands with more dangers than any man. So no stranger in distress will ever seek my help in vain — nor shall you. I know I am mortal, and my share of what tomorrow brings is no greater than yours.

before: OEDIPUS. Shameless railer — do you think this abuse defames my grey hairs more than your own? Murder and incest — you blurt out these horrors as charges against me, and I have borne them all, no willing sinner. So it pleased the gods, angry perhaps with my sinful race of old, since they could find no sin in me myself for which in retribution I was doomed to trespass this way against myself and mine. Answer me this: if by some oracle my father was destined to a bloody end at a son's hand, how can this reflect on me — on me, then unborn, begotten by no father, conceived in no mother's womb? And if, born to misery, as I was born, I met my father, not knowing who he was or what I was doing, and killed him, how can you justly blame that utterly unconscious hand? As for my mother — wretch, are you not ashamed to force out of me the story of her marriage, since she was your own sister? That marriage I will proclaim at once. I will speak: your lewd and impious words have broken all the bonds of silence. She was, alas, my mother. I did not know it; neither did she. And she, my mother, bore children to the son she herself had borne — a shameful birth. But this much I know: you slander her and me deliberately, while I married without knowing and speak now unwillingly. No — neither in this marriage nor in the deed you keep throwing in my face — a murdered father — shall I be held to blame. Come, answer me one question, if you can: if someone tried right now to take your life, would you — man of justice — first inquire whether the attacker was perhaps your father, or would you turn on him at once? As you love your life, you would turn on your attacker, without stopping to debate, provided the law backed you. Such was my case, and such the position the gods reduced me to. And I think my father, if he could come back to life, would not disagree. Yet you, who are not just but a man who will stop at nothing if it serves his argument, reproach me with this in front of these men. It suits you to praise great Theseus's name and Athens as a wisely governed State. And yet in your flatteries one thing is missing: if any land knows how to render the gods their proper rites, it is Athens most of all. This is the land from which you tried to steal their aged suppliant, and from which you have carried off my daughters. So I turn to those goddesses here, I call on them, I invoke their help to champion my cause — so you may learn what breed of men watches over this State.
